canonical_statement: Multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa is defined as non-susceptibility to at least one antibiotic in at least three antibiotic classes in which susceptibility is generally expected.

source_anchor.paragraph: Section 4 opening definition: MDR P. aeruginosa

canonical_statement: Difficult-to-treat resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa is defined as non-susceptibility to aztreonam, cefepime, ceftazidime, ciprofloxacin, imipenem, levofloxacin, meropenem, and piperacillin-tazobactam.

source_anchor.paragraph: Section 4 opening definition: DTR P. aeruginosa

canonical_statement: MDR and DTR P. aeruginosa generally result from combinations of resistance mechanisms including porin loss or alteration, PDC/AmpC changes, efflux upregulation, PBP mutations, ESBLs, and occasionally carbapenemases.

Four newer beta-lactam agents with potential activity against DTR P. aeruginosa are available in the United States: cefiderocol, ceftazidime-avibactam, ceftolozane-tazobactam, and imipenem-relebactam.
The panel encourages susceptibility testing for all four newer beta-lactam agents when DTR P. aeruginosa is identified because activity varies among agents.
When a P. aeruginosa isolate is susceptible to both traditional non-carbapenem antipseudomonal beta-lactams and carbapenems, the panel prefers a traditional non-carbapenem beta-lactam.

For carbapenem-nonsusceptible P. aeruginosa that remains susceptible to a traditional beta-lactam, the panel suggests a high-dose prolonged-infusion regimen of the susceptible traditional beta-lactam.

For critically ill patients or patients with poor source control whose carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa remains susceptible to traditional beta-lactams, a susceptible newer beta-lactam is also considered reasonable.

Carbapenem treatment of P. aeruginosa infections has been associated with more frequent emergence of resistance during therapy than treatment with other traditional antipseudomonal beta-lactams, without improved clinical outcomes.

Wild-type P. aeruginosa has higher upper-end MIC distributions than wild-type E. coli for cefepime, ceftazidime, and piperacillin-tazobactam; cited upper values are 8, 8, and 16/4 mcg/mL for P. aeruginosa versus 0.125, 1, and 8/4 mcg/mL for E. coli.

Clinical data cited by the guidance suggest improved outcomes with prolonged beta-lactam infusions of approximately 3–4 hours compared with standard infusions of approximately 30 minutes for P. aeruginosa infections.
At least 40% of carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa isolates are reported to remain susceptible to other traditional antipseudomonal beta-lactams.
Carbapenem resistance with retained susceptibility to traditional beta-lactams is most commonly attributed to reduced expression or alteration of the OprD porin.

For carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa that remains susceptible to a traditional beta-lactam, the panel prefers high-dose extended-infusion treatment with the susceptible traditional beta-lactam; cefepime 2 g IV every 8 hours infused over at least 3 hours is given as an example.
Among 767 P. aeruginosa bacteremia episodes, resistance emerging within 30 days was reported in 12% with ceftazidime, 27% with imipenem, 15% with meropenem, and 8% with piperacillin-tazobactam.
The panel encourages repeat antimicrobial susceptibility testing for subsequent P. aeruginosa isolates recovered from the same patient.
For cUTI caused by DTR P. aeruginosa, cefiderocol, ceftazidime-avibactam, ceftolozane-tazobactam, and imipenem-relebactam are preferred options without an order of preference.
Once-daily amikacin or tobramycin are alternative treatments for cUTI caused by DTR P. aeruginosa.

The four preferred newer beta-lactams for DTR P. aeruginosa cUTI are supported by trials demonstrating non-inferiority to standard comparator regimens, but available data do not support preferring one of the four over another.

The panel suggests considering preservation of cefiderocol for other antimicrobial-resistant infections because of its distinctive activity against NDM-producing Enterobacterales and non-fermenters beyond P. aeruginosa.
Aminoglycosides may be effective for DTR P. aeruginosa cUTI because of high renal parenchymal concentrations, but duration-dependent nephrotoxicity is an important limitation.

Plazomicin does not provide improved in vitro activity against P. aeruginosa compared with traditional aminoglycosides, and neither CLSI nor FDA P. aeruginosa breakpoints for plazomicin are available.

For the rare uUTI caused by DTR P. aeruginosa, potential options listed by the panel include single-dose amikacin or tobramycin, cefiderocol, ceftazidime-avibactam, ceftolozane-tazobactam, imipenem-relebactam, or colistin.
Colistin, but not polymyxin B, is considered a potential option for DTR P. aeruginosa uUTI because colistimethate is converted to active colistin within the urinary tract.
For DTR P. aeruginosa infections outside the urinary tract, ceftazidime-avibactam, ceftolozane-tazobactam, and imipenem-relebactam are preferred agents, while cefiderocol is an alternative.
Among preferred agents for DTR P. aeruginosa pneumonia, the panel prefers ceftolozane-tazobactam.
Trials of ceftazidime-avibactam, ceftolozane-tazobactam, and imipenem-relebactam have shown favorable pneumonia outcomes, although few enrolled patients had DTR P. aeruginosa.

Observational studies cited by the guidance consistently report better outcomes with newer beta-lactams for MDR or DTR P. aeruginosa than with alternative regimens typically based on polymyxins, aminoglycosides, and/or carbapenems.
In a randomized trial subgroup of 22 patients with carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa infection, survival was 82% with cefiderocol and 82% with alternative therapy that was primarily polymyxin based.

population.label: Patients with carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa infection

canonical_statement: In a randomized trial subgroup of 16 patients with carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa bacteremia, 30-day survival was 75% in both the cefiderocol and traditional-therapy arms.

population.label: Patients with carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa bacteremia

canonical_statement: Observational studies of cefiderocol for DTR P. aeruginosa are generally limited by small samples and lack of comparator groups, limiting conclusions about relative effectiveness.
Observational comparisons of ceftazidime-avibactam versus ceftolozane-tazobactam for DTR P. aeruginosa have not identified a difference in 30-day survival.

In the largest observational comparison cited, patients with MDR P. aeruginosa pneumonia had clinical success of 51% (89/175) with ceftazidime-avibactam versus 63% (110/175) with ceftolozane-tazobactam.

population.label: Patients with MDR P. aeruginosa pneumonia

canonical_statement: Across the overall cohort of the same observational study, 30-day recurrent infection occurred in 21% (44/210) with ceftazidime-avibactam versus 15% (31/210) with ceftolozane-tazobactam.

population.label: Patients with MDR P. aeruginosa pneumonia or bacteremia in the overall comparative cohort

canonical_statement: A separate observational study reported recurrent pneumonia in 18% (21/117) of ceftazidime-avibactam recipients versus 8% (6/80) of ceftolozane-tazobactam recipients.

population.label: Patients with P. aeruginosa pneumonia in an observational comparison

canonical_statement: In pneumonia, ceftolozane epithelial lining fluid concentrations are reported at about 50% of plasma concentrations and remain above 4 mcg/mL for 100% of the dosing interval.
Ceftazidime and avibactam each achieve epithelial lining fluid concentrations of approximately 30% of plasma concentrations.

DTR P. aeruginosa isolates may be less likely to test susceptible to imipenem-relebactam than to ceftolozane-tazobactam or ceftazidime-avibactam, and clinical outcomes data for imipenem-relebactam are less extensive.
In an observational study of 63 patients with MDR P. aeruginosa infections treated with imipenem-relebactam, 30-day survival was approximately 80%.

population.label: Patients with MDR P. aeruginosa infections

canonical_statement: For KPC-producing P. aeruginosa infections, cefiderocol, ceftazidime-avibactam, and imipenem-relebactam are preferred options, with selection informed by susceptibility testing.
For P. aeruginosa producing NDM, VIM, or IMP metallo-beta-lactamases, cefiderocol is the preferred agent.

Carbapenemase-producing carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa is reported to account for approximately 69% of isolates in Latin America, 57% in Asia, and 50% in Southern Europe, while remaining uncommon in the United States.
A 2022–2023 United States outbreak of VIM- and GES-producing P. aeruginosa linked to contaminated artificial tears caused 81 infections, with permanent vision loss in 17% and death in 5% of cases.

population.label: Patients in a U.S. VIM- and GES-producing P. aeruginosa outbreak

concept.text: VIM- and GES-producing P. aeruginosa outbreak exposure

canonical_statement: Some GES alleles such as GES-5 have carbapenemase activity, whereas others such as GES-1 do not.
FDA-cleared multiplex assays can detect KPC, VIM, IMP, NDM, and OXA-48 carbapenemases from specimens including blood cultures and respiratory samples.
Ceftolozane-tazobactam is not suggested for KPC-producing P. aeruginosa because tazobactam does not inhibit KPC enzymes.
Among 44 KPC-producing P. aeruginosa isolates, 48% were resistant to ceftazidime-avibactam and 75% were resistant to imipenem-relebactam.

canonical_statement: When an MBL is identified in P. aeruginosa, ceftazidime-avibactam, ceftolozane-tazobactam, and imipenem-relebactam are not suggested because their beta-lactamase inhibitors do not inhibit MBLs.

Concurrent resistance to ceftazidime-avibactam, ceftolozane-tazobactam, and imipenem-relebactam in DTR P. aeruginosa should raise suspicion for MBL production when carbapenemase testing is unavailable.
Clinical outcomes data for cefiderocol in MBL-producing P. aeruginosa remain limited, and cefiderocol-resistant MBL-producing isolates have been reported.

source_anchor.paragraph: Question 4.4 — Rationale: cefiderocol limitations in MBL

canonical_statement: Identification of a carbapenemase gene does not replace phenotypic susceptibility testing; AST for preferred agents should still be obtained.
Aztreonam-avibactam is not suggested for MBL-producing P. aeruginosa because activity is limited and neither CLSI nor FDA susceptibility breakpoints are available.
Ceftazidime-avibactam plus aztreonam is suggested only when resistance precludes cefiderocol for MBL-producing P. aeruginosa; supporting clinical data are limited to small case series.
The panel estimates that treatment-emergent resistance occurs in approximately 20% of DTR P. aeruginosa isolates treated with newer beta-lactam agents.

Among 167 U.S. DTR P. aeruginosa isolates collected in 2019–2021, susceptibility was 50% to ceftazidime-avibactam, 74% to ceftolozane-tazobactam, and 37% to imipenem-relebactam; cefiderocol was not evaluated.
Among 154 DTR P. aeruginosa isolates collected in 2020–2023, susceptibility was 99% to cefiderocol, 61% to ceftazidime-avibactam, 71% to ceftolozane-tazobactam, and 62% to imipenem-relebactam.
Across surveillance studies cited by the guidance, cefiderocol generally has the highest likelihood of in vitro activity against MDR and DTR P. aeruginosa.
Cross-resistance between ceftazidime-avibactam and ceftolozane-tazobactam exceeds 50%.
Emergence of non-susceptibility during ceftazidime-avibactam or ceftolozane-tazobactam therapy has been reported in approximately 24% of DTR P. aeruginosa infections.
Cefiderocol MIC increases have been observed in approximately 15% of P. aeruginosa isolates after exposure to ceftazidime-avibactam or ceftolozane-tazobactam.

canonical_statement: Limited data suggest that fewer than 10% of P. aeruginosa isolates develop cefiderocol resistance during cefiderocol treatment.
Across two clinical trials including 50 patients with P. aeruginosa infections treated with imipenem-relebactam, no treatment-emergent imipenem-relebactam resistance was observed.

population.label: Patients with P. aeruginosa infections treated with imipenem-relebactam

canonical_statement: In two observational studies including 46 patients treated with imipenem-relebactam, treatment-emergent non-susceptibility developed in approximately 24% of patients.

population.label: Patients treated with imipenem-relebactam in two observational studies

canonical_statement: Repeat AST is supported for P. aeruginosa isolates recovered during therapy or when patients re-present with suspected DTR P. aeruginosa infection.

Combination antibiotic therapy is not suggested for DTR P. aeruginosa infection once in vitro susceptibility to cefiderocol, ceftazidime-avibactam, ceftolozane-tazobactam, or imipenem-relebactam has been confirmed.

Empiric combination therapy may be reasonable to increase the likelihood of initial active coverage in patients at risk for DTR P. aeruginosa, but continuation after confirmation of an active beta-lactam is not supported.

source_anchor.paragraph: Question 4.6 — Rationale: empiric versus definitive combination therapy

canonical_statement: Available evidence has not shown better clinical outcomes with continued combination therapy than with active beta-lactam monotherapy and indicates more antibiotic-related adverse events.

source_anchor.paragraph: Question 4.6 — Rationale: combination therapy outcomes and harms

canonical_statement: Observational studies cited by the guidance have not identified a survival benefit from combination therapy for DTR P. aeruginosa.

If no beta-lactam is susceptible, the panel allows consideration of tobramycin, if susceptible, combined with the newer beta-lactam whose MIC is closest to its susceptibility breakpoint, while noting that outcome data supporting this strategy are lacking.
Aminoglycoside monotherapy is not suggested for DTR P. aeruginosa infections outside the urinary tract because pharmacodynamic target attainment for bactericidal activity is suboptimal.
If tobramycin susceptibility is not demonstrated and no beta-lactam is active, polymyxin B may be considered in combination with a newer beta-lactam.

canonical_statement: For infections outside the urinary tract, polymyxin B is preferred over colistin because it is administered in active form, yields more reliable plasma concentrations, and may have lower nephrotoxicity.

canonical_statement: The panel does not suggest routine nebulized antibiotics for DTR P. aeruginosa pneumonia when an active systemic beta-lactam has been confirmed in vitro.
Three cited randomized trials evaluated adjunctive nebulized antibiotics versus placebo in adults with gram-negative pneumonia while allowing concomitant systemic antibiotics.

The three adjunctive nebulized-antibiotic trials included 100 patients receiving nebulized colistin (34% with P. aeruginosa), 142 receiving nebulized amikacin/fosfomycin (22% with P. aeruginosa), and 508 receiving nebulized amikacin (32% with P. aeruginosa).
None of the three adjunctive nebulized-antibiotic trials demonstrated improvement in clinically meaningful outcomes, including survival, either overall or in subgroups with drug-resistant pathogens.
Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of adjunctive inhaled antibiotics for pneumonia have not identified a survival benefit, although some reported modest improvement in clinical response.
PK/PD modeling cited by the guidance suggests that aerosolized antibiotics can achieve high epithelial lining fluid concentrations.
The guidance identifies inadequate penetration into consolidated lung parenchyma and heterogeneous airway drug distribution as factors that may limit the effectiveness of nebulized antibiotics.
